vis: opened hummingbird, labels HEART / MUSCLE / TONGUE
text: This is a hummingbird. One of the smallest birds on Earth. But inside this tiny body is one of the most powerful engines in nature. Today, we're opening it up, one part at a time.

vis: bird on a scale vs a coin: 3 G
text: First, how small is it? A ruby-throated hummingbird weighs about three grams. That's about as much as a single coin.

vis: bee hummingbird next to a real bee: SMALLEST BIRD
text: And the smallest one of all lives in Cuba. It's called the bee hummingbird. It's only about five centimeters long. The smallest bird in the world.

vis: wings blur, counter spins: 50 PER SECOND
text: Now look at the wings. A hummingbird flaps them about fifty times every second. Some tiny hummingbirds flap up to eighty. That's so fast your eyes only see a blur. And that blur makes the humming sound that gives this bird its name.

vis: wing tip draws a sideways 8: FIGURE 8
text: But they don't just flap up and down. The wings sweep forward and back, tracing a sideways figure eight in the air.

vis: shoulder joint glows, wing flips over: SHOULDER SPINS
text: The secret is in the shoulder. A hummingbird can twist its wing almost all the way over. So the wing pushes air down on the way forward, and pushes air down again on the way back.

vis: three arrows around the bird: HOVER / BACKWARD / UPSIDE DOWN
text: That's why a hummingbird can do things no other bird can. It can hover in one spot like a helicopter. It can fly backwards. It can even flip upside down for a moment.

vis: chest opens, MUSCLE fills the chest: 1/4
text: All that flapping needs power. So let's open the chest. Huge flight muscles fill most of it. They can make up about a quarter of the whole bird's weight.

vis: HEART beats fast, counter: 1,200 BEATS / MINUTE vs YOU 70
text: And right in the middle is the heart. Compared to its size, it's huge. A hummingbird's heart can beat more than twelve hundred times a minute. Yours beats about seventy.

vis: lungs puff fast: 250 BREATHS
text: It breathes fast too. Even resting, a hummingbird can take about two hundred and fifty breaths every minute.

vis: engine with a FUEL gauge dropping fast: FASTEST ENGINE
text: Scientists say hummingbirds burn energy faster than almost any other animal. It's like a tiny engine running at full speed all day long. And an engine like that needs a lot of fuel.

vis: beak opens, a long TONGUE shoots out
text: So where does the fuel come from? Flowers. Let's look inside the beak. Hiding in there is a very long tongue.

vis: tongue tip splits in two, fringes open and grab nectar: FORKED TONGUE
text: The tip of the tongue is split in two. When it dips into nectar, the edges open up like tiny brushes and grab the sweet liquid. Then they snap shut and pull it back.

vis: tongue in and out, counter: 15 LICKS / SECOND
text: And it does this fast. Around fifteen licks every second.

vis: flower counter climbs: 1,000+ FLOWERS A DAY
text: A hummingbird visits hundreds, even thousands, of flowers every day. And in one day, it can drink more than its own body weight in nectar.

vis: stomach with a sugar cube and a tiny bug: SUGAR + BUGS
text: But sugar alone isn't enough. To grow strong, hummingbirds also catch tiny insects and spiders. Sugar for energy, bugs for building the body.

vis: flowers get dusted with yellow powder: POLLEN TAXI
text: And while it drinks, something else happens. Yellow pollen sticks to its head and beak. At the next flower, the pollen rubs off. That helps flowers make seeds. So the hummingbird is a tiny taxi for flowers.

vis: brain glows, map of flowers with timers: SUPER MEMORY
text: Now the brain. For its size, the part that handles memory is very big. A hummingbird can remember which flowers it already visited, and how long until they fill up with nectar again.

vis: eye, rainbow with an extra purple band: SEES MORE COLORS
text: And its eyes can see colors we can't, like ultraviolet. To a hummingbird, flowers can glow with patterns that are invisible to us.

vis: night background, bird puffs up, thermometer drops: TORPOR
text: But here's a problem. At night, a hummingbird can't eat. With an engine that hungry, it could run out of fuel before morning. So it does something amazing. It goes into a deep sleep called torpor.

vis: heart counter slows from 1,200 to 50, ZZZ
text: Its body cools down, a lot. Its heart slows from more than a thousand beats a minute to around fifty. It almost switches itself off. In the morning, it warms back up and gets going again.

vis: tiny feet, a crossed-out walking bird: CAN'T WALK
text: Now look down at the feet. They're tiny. Good for holding on to a branch, but a hummingbird can't really walk or hop. If it wants to move, even a few centimeters, it flies.

vis: throat sparkles red then turns dark as it tilts: NO PAINT!
text: Next, that shiny red throat. Here's a surprise. There's no red paint in those feathers. The feathers are built with tiny layers that bounce light. Turn the bird a little, and the red flashes on. Turn it again, and it goes dark.

vis: bird dives in a U-shape, tail fins make a CHIRP
text: Some male hummingbirds use that shine to show off. Anna's hummingbird climbs high, then dives straight down at nearly a hundred kilometers per hour. At the bottom, its tail feathers buzz and make a loud chirp.

vis: map: fat bird on one side, ocean crossing: 800 KM NONSTOP
text: Hummingbirds are also amazing travelers. Before its trip, a ruby-throated hummingbird eats so much it almost doubles its weight. Then it flies across the Gulf of Mexico. About eight hundred kilometers, nonstop, without landing once.

vis: map: Alaska → Mexico line: RUFOUS, 6,000+ KM
text: And the rufous hummingbird flies from Alaska all the way to Mexico. More than six thousand kilometers. For a bird this small, that's one of the longest trips in the animal world.

vis: nest the size of half a walnut, spider web threads: SPIDER SILK NEST
text: Now, the nest. It's about the size of half a walnut. The mother builds it with soft plant fluff, and holds it together with spider silk. The silk stretches, so the nest grows as the babies grow.

vis: two eggs next to jelly beans: 2 EGGS
text: Inside are usually two eggs, each about the size of a jelly bean. The mother raises the chicks all by herself.

vis: map of the Americas lights up: ONLY IN THE AMERICAS, 360+ KINDS
text: There are more than three hundred and sixty kinds of hummingbirds. And all of them live only in the Americas, from Alaska to the tip of South America.

vis: sword-billed hummingbird: BEAK LONGER THAN BODY
text: One of them, the sword-billed hummingbird, has a beak longer than the rest of its body. It's perfect for reaching deep inside long flowers.

vis: opened hummingbird with all labels, then question card
text: So that's a hummingbird. Wings that spin at the shoulder. A heart that beats twelve hundred times a minute. A brushy tongue, a super memory, and a body that can almost switch off at night. Tiny, but packed with power. What should we open next? Tell us in the comments.
